Iran’s currency hits record low

Iran’s currency, the rial, hit a record low on Wednesday.

Traders in the Tehran market exchanged 2.20 million rials for one US dollar. That was nearly 10% higher than last week’s record, set on August 25, when one dollar was sold at 2.02 million rials.

The currency had already been under pressure before the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on February 28 as Iran battled double-digit inflation and negative growth.

The rial has repeatedly hit new lows since the conflict started more than six months ago. The troubled currency ​has lost about half of its value ⁠in a year ​of tightening ​US sanctions ​and American ​and ‌Israeli attacks.

The Latest, the evening edition of Today in Focus, features a conversation between host Lucy Hough and Middle East correspondent Will Christou about the conflict between the US and Iran.

During the eight-minute update, they talk about Tehran accusing Washington of a ‘war crime’ after a missile blast reportedly killed wedding guests, including a young child.

Christou talks about how the latest exchange of strikes are part of a “cycle of escalation” in the tension between the two nations.

Chinese president Xi Jinping urged Middle Eastern countries on Wednesday to oppose “external interference” and said Beijing was ready to work with regional states to safeguard maritime shipping, jeopardised by the US-Iran war.

Xi’s remarks to his Egyptian counterpart Abdel Fattah al-Sisi, on his first visit to Cairo in a decade, come as Beijing seeks a greater foothold in the region, expanding investment while managing fallout from the six-month conflict.

“We must uphold the principle that the people of the Middle East are the masters of their own affairs, oppose external interference (and) support regional countries in strengthening dialogue on peace and security,” Xi said in a meeting with Sisi, according to Chinese state news agency Xinhua.

Trump suggests strait of Hormuz could be renamed 'Trump strait'

US president Donald Trump has suggested renaming the strait of Hormuz ‘Trump strait’.

In a post on his Truth Social network, he wrote:

Now that we have it under U.S.A. control, should we change the name Hormuz Strait to TRUMP STRAIT??? Like America itself, it would be “hotter” than ever before!

Now that we have it under U.S.A. control, should we change the name Hormuz Strait to TRUMP STRAIT??? Like America itself, it would be “hotter” than ever before!

Trump has in recent weeks repeatedly pressed a threat to claim sovereignty over the strait of Hormuz, even posting a map showing the waterway as a “new US territory.”

Iranians expressed regret at the return to hostilities including the deaths at the wedding.

Hossein Moazami, 50, who is self-employed, called the attacks “truly distressing”. “I hope they all return to the negotiating table, because the only people suffering from this are the Iranian people,” he said.

“The Americans are on the other side of the world, and nothing happens to them.”

A video shared by an Iranian government account showed debris and damage at what it said was the wedding site in Sirik after the US strike, with people heard screaming in the background.

“It is a very saddening incident … Thank God the casualties were not higher,” Ali Mallahi, father of the bride and owner of the building that was hit, said in a video carried by state TV.

Top diplomats in Egypt and Qatar have called for the US and Iran to return to the negotiating table in line with their collapsed ceasefire deal.

Foreign minister Badr Abdelatty of Egypt spoke by phone on Wednesday with his Qatari counterpart Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani.

The ministers warned that the ongoing escalation threatens “dire consequences on the region’s security and stability,” the Egyptian foreign ministry said.

Iranian border ⁠guards have seized a vessel with ⁠382,000 ⁠litres of ​smuggled fuel in the northern Gulf, ⁠and arrested its foreign crew ⁠of 11, the state broadcaster ​IRIB ‌reported ‌on Wednesday, without giving ‌the nationality of the detained.

Iran, which has some of the world’s lowest fuel ‌prices due to heavy subsidies and a ​sharp fall in the value of its national currency, ⁠has been seeking to ​curb ​widespread fuel ​smuggling by land to ​neighbouring ‌countries ​and ​by sea to Gulf states.

My colleague, William Christou, has the full report on the missile blast that killed at least four people and injured 68 at a wedding in a private home in southern Iran. You can read that here:

Trump nominates loyalist Hung Cao to be permanent navy secretary amid increased attacks on Iran

Donald Trump has picked acting navy secretary Hung Cao to take on the job permanently amid concerns that some sailors have been stretched to the limit during his Iran war.

“I am pleased to nominate a true WARRIOR,” Trump wrote on social media, pushing the Senate “to confirm this Warfighter, ASAP.”

Cao has been serving as acting navy secretary since John Phelan departed the job unexpectedly and without explanation in late April. Unlike Phelan, who had not served in the military or had a civilian leadership role in the service, Cao spent 25 years in the navy as a special operations officer and went on to serve with Seal teams and special forces in Iraq and Afghanistan.

Cao on social media called it the “honor of a lifetime to lead the great warriors of the Navy and Marine Corps team”.

For more US politics news, my colleague Victoria Bekiempis has the latest updates on our live blog here:

Here is a video featuring clips shared by Iranian media of the reported US strike in Sirik in the south of the country that hit a wedding ceremony, killing four people and wounding dozens more. US central command (Centcom) denied targeting civilians and also released footage purportedly showing missile and drone strikes on Iranian military sites.

articles.title: JD Vance says he’s doing ‘God’s work – and if that leads to the end times, OK’
articles.excerpt: Vice-president says on evangelical podcast he would feel ‘not shocked if the antichrist was walking among us’
articles.content:
Vice-president says on evangelical podcast he would feel ‘not shocked if the antichrist was walking among us’

JD Vance has said he is “doing as much of God’s work as possible” and that he is OK “if that leads to the end times”, which he says “are coming”.

The US vice-president made the comments during a Monday podcast interview with Bryce Crawford, a 22-year-old evangelical host with over a million YouTube followers and videos featuring sensationalist headlines including “Preaching the gospel in Chicago’s deadliest neighborhood” and “Debating a ‘gay’ pastor”.

Speaking about the Christian prophetic notion that the world as humanity knows it will end one day, Vance said: “Do I think we are in the end times? I don’t know.

“While I’m fascinated by it, I think that focusing on it too much can be very bad,” he said, adding that if his work “leads to the end times, OK, and if that leads to … us building a better world that thrives and survives for a very long time after I’m gone, that’s great, too”.

Vance, who published a spiritual memoir earlier this summer about his conversion to Catholicism, said: “I think you got to just kinda try and have an attitude of: the end times may be coming, in fact they are coming, it’s just a question of whether they’re coming thousands of years down the road, or a few months down the road.”

He said: “I think there are things about the world that make me feel, like, not shocked if the antichrist was walking among us.”

Vance pointed to artificial intelligence, using the example of an acquaintance who uses AI as a marriage counselor, which he described as “kind of satanic”. He said: “When you completely divorce the human from the social element that God made us for … that’s very bad.”

In response to a question about whether he had ever been in a room that was “spiritually dark”, Vance said he had “been in meetings with world leaders where various issues are being discussed, and somebody will say something or somebody will make an observation, and I’ll feel some darkness about it”.

“It sets off every spiritual alarm bell in my body,” he added.

Vance also defended Donald Trump’s controversial depiction of himself as Jesus in an AI-generated photo, subsequently deleted, that the president posted earlier this year, which Crawford said “made me upset”.

“The president didn’t mean any offense. Obviously, he loves Christians … Did Donald Trump mean to post a meme of himself as God? No. The president has a good sense of humor. He did not mean to mock or mimic God. That’s just not who he is,” Vance said, adding that Trump is “a backslapper” and “a bit of a ball buster”.

Following outrage from Christian supporters, Trump deleted the photo and insisted that the photo was “supposed to be me as a doctor making people feel better”.

articles.title: A First Look at Michael J. Fox and Harrison Ford’s Next Must-See Project
articles.excerpt: The Shrinking stars have paired up again on a campaign for the Michael J. Fox Foundation.
articles.content:
The Shrinking stars have paired up again on a campaign for the Michael J. Fox Foundation.

Michael J. Fox and Harrison Ford might both be nominated for Emmy Awards for their work on Shrinking, but that isn’t where the collaboration between the two screen legends—who both play characters with Parkinson’s on the hit series—ends. The pair also appear together in a new campaign for the Michael J. Fox Foundation, the 26-year-old nonprofit focused on Parkinson’s, and T&C has a first look here.

The video, which was created by Maximum Effort, the entertainment company helmed by MJFF board member Ryan Reynolds, focuses on the conversations we have around issues like Parkinson’s and what it means to actually offer support to friends and family members experiencing it—which might look different than you’d think.

“As I’ve grown older, I’ve realized social connections mean so much—Parkinson’s or not,” Fox tells T&C. “Shooting Shrinking with Harrison and the friendship we've developed reminded me how important those connections are. I hope the authenticity of our friendship comes through in the campaign. We’re using humor and banter to get at what matters. But there’s tremendous seriousness of purpose behind it. We want the community to know that as long as Parkinson’s exists, the Foundation will be here to support everyone living with the disease. The challenges are real, but knowing you’ve got someone in your corner makes a huge difference. And that’s why this campaign is so important.”

Ford says, “Michael has a remarkable way of making difficult things easier to talk about, and that’s part of what makes working with him and being his friend so special. We wanted to bring some of that honesty and humor to a conversation that a lot of people may not know how to have.”

In addition to his Emmy nomination for his work on Shrinking, Fox will also be honored with this year’s Bob Hope Humanitarian Award, a special accolade previously awarded to Oprah Winfrey, Danny Thomas, George Clooney, Sean Penn, and Ted Danson and Mary Steenburgen. Of course, Fox’s philanthropy is widely known; he was on the cover of T&C’s 2023 November issue in support of his philanthropic work, which stems from the diagnosis he received when he was just 29 years old. For that story, he said, “When I went public, I felt like I stood there naked in the town square and said, ‘Look at me. This is what it is.’ What I didn’t realize was how many other people had been dying to do that.”

In recent years, the foundation had reportedly allocated more money to Parkinson’s research than the U.S. government and as of 2022 was supporting more than $3 billion in research programs—and this new campaign is the next step toward reaching its goals. Debi Brooks, the foundation’s CEO and cofounder, says, “The world has taken notice of the special relationship between Michael and Harrison. Our brand campaign combines humor and compassion to highlight the very serious purpose behind our work. It has been a joy to see these Hollywood giants come together to capture attention and channel it toward what matters most: bringing greater awareness and support to people and families living with Parkinson’s.”

Asked what people can say to a friend, Fox shares this advice: ‘Just saying, ‘I got you, I have your back,and I always will’ means everything. Keep showing up!”

Adam Rathe is Town & Country's Deputy Features Director, covering film, theater, books, travel, art, philanthropy, and a range of other subjects.
